questions.q: Cyclohexanone reacts with Ph₃P=CH₂. The organic product is:
questions.explain: The Wittig reaction forms the new C=C exactly where the C=O was, so only the exocyclic alkene is formed, with Ph₃P=O. The ring alkene is the trap: it is what the Grignard-then-dehydration route can give, as part of a mixture of isomers.

questions.q: The driving force of the Wittig reaction is:
options: Relief of strain in the ylide
Formation of the very strong P=O bond
questions.explain: The four-membered oxaphosphetane breaks apart into the alkene and triphenylphosphine oxide, and the strong P=O bond in Ph₃P=O drives this step. Loss of N₂ is the driving force of the Wolff–Kishner reduction, not the Wittig.

questions.q: A stabilised ylide such as Ph₃P=CH–COOC₂H₅ reacts with an aldehyde. The alkene formed is mainly:
options: A 1:1 E/Z mixture in every case
questions.explain: Stabilised ylides (R = ester or ketone) are less reactive and give mainly E-alkenes. Non-stabilised ylides (R = alkyl) give mainly Z-alkenes, and aryl (semi-stabilised) ylides often give mixtures.

questions.q: Which alkene CANNOT be made satisfactorily by a Wittig reaction?
questions.explain: 2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene is tetrasubstituted, and steric hindrance prevents its formation by the Wittig route. Mono-, di- and trisubstituted alkenes such as styrene (benzaldehyde + Ph₃P=CH₂) are fine.
